name: Mangan
tagline: District town of North Sikkim and its large cardamom
meta_description: Mangan, North Sikkim's district town: large cardamom farms, the bazaar, Dzongu permits, shared jeeps from Gangtok, rooms and costs, plus road status.
summary: Mangan is the headquarters of Mangan district, formerly North Sikkim, a small town at about 956 m above the Teesta, 65 km from Gangtok. It calls itself the large cardamom capital, issues Dzongu permits and makes a cheap base for Singhik and Dzongu. No permit needed for Indians. Check current status before you travel.

local_story.title: The cardamom town that named a district
paras: For most of its history Mangan was a small Lepcha and Nepali village on the slope above the Teesta, surrounded by forest and farms. It grew into the administrative centre of North Sikkim after Sikkim joined India in 1975, and in 2021 the state renamed its districts after their headquarters, so North Sikkim became Mangan district. It is the largest district in Sikkim by area and one of the least populated in India, and Mangan town had about 4,600 people at the 2011 census.

The money here grows in the shade. Large cardamom, the smoky black pod used in Indian garams masalas, is planted under alder and other trees on the moist slopes around Mangan and Dzongu, and the district has long described itself as the large cardamom capital of the world. Harvest runs from late August into autumn, when the pods are dried over wood fires in small smokehouses called bhattis. Since Sikkim became a fully organic farming state in 2016, Mangan's farmers sell their cardamom, ginger and oranges with that label.

did_you_know: Mangan district, renamed from North Sikkim, is Sikkim's largest district by area and among the least populous districts in India.
Large cardamom pods are cured over wood fires in small kilns called bhattis, which gives them their smoky taste.
Kanchenjunga can be seen clearly from Singhik, just 4 km beyond Mangan, on clear mornings from October to April.
intro: Mangan is a working town, not a resort. Government offices, a hospital, schools, banks and a short bazaar line the road above the Teesta. North Sikkim tours pass through around lunchtime and rarely stop, but for budget travellers Mangan is useful: shared jeeps from Gangtok, cheap rooms, Dzongu permits and a choice of walks.

Stay a night and you see a side of North Sikkim that package tours miss: farmers carrying sacks of cardamom to market, school buses, Lepcha families from Dzongu shopping across the river, and the evening light on the Teesta gorge. Singhik's Kanchenjunga view is 4 km up the road. Since the 2023 flood, the Teesta road below Mangan has had closures; check current status before you travel.
facts: Large cardamom, district HQ, Dzongu permits
Jio, Airtel and BSNL work in town

highlights.title: Cardamom country
highlights.text: Large cardamom grows under shade trees on the slopes around Mangan. Ask in the bazaar or your hotel about a short walk to a farm or a drying kiln, especially from September to November.

highlights.title: The bazaar
highlights.text: A short, busy strip of shops, eateries and offices. Buy cardamom, local ginger and seasonal oranges, eat momos with the office crowd, and watch Dzongu families come in to shop.

highlights.title: Gateway to Dzongu
highlights.text: Mangan is where Dzongu permits are usually issued and where you find taxis across the Teesta to Lepcha villages such as Lingthem and Passingdang.

highlights.title: Singhik's Kanchenjunga
highlights.text: A 4 km walk or short taxi ride up the road leads to Singhik's viewpoint for Kanchenjunga and Siniolchu. Go at dawn from October to April.

highlights.title: A cheap break on the long drive
highlights.text: If you are travelling independently, Mangan splits the trip north into easier days and costs far less than a night in Lachung.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps leave Gangtok's Vajra taxi stand at Maarchak, about 3 km north of the centre, for Mangan from early morning until early afternoon, when full. About ₹200–300 a seat, 2.5–3 hours via Kabi and Phodong. Return jeeps leave Mangan in the morning.
A small car from Gangtok to Mangan costs about ₹2,500–3,500 one way. Useful for families or if you want to stop at Kabi Lungchok, Seven Sisters falls and Phodong on the way.
Lachen and Lachung tours pass through Mangan around midday. Some agents can pick up or drop off here if you have arranged it beforehand.

where_to_stay: Mangan has a handful of small hotels and lodges in and around the bazaar, used mainly by officials and business travellers, with simple rooms at roughly ₹1,200–2,500. Ask for a room facing the valley. For a view, many travellers prefer Singhik, 4 km up the road, where the Sikkim Tourism lodge looks across to Kanchenjunga. For homestays, cross into Dzongu with a permit and stay with a Lepcha family.
tips: Go to the Vajra stand in Gangtok before 9 am for the best chance of a shared jeep to Mangan.
Ask at the district office early in the day about Dzongu permits; offices close by late afternoon and on holidays.
Buy cardamom from a shop that lets you see and smell the pods; good pods are plump and smoky.
Carry cash for Dzongu and beyond; Mangan's ATMs are the last reliable ones heading north.
Avoid travelling the Gangtok–Mangan road after dark in the monsoon.

experiences.title: A walk through a large cardamom farm
experiences.cost: Free to ₹300 tip for a local guide
experiences.summary: Large cardamom, the smoky black pod of Indian kitchens, grows under shade trees on the slopes around Mangan. Ask locally for a farmer who will walk you through the plants and, from September to November, show you the harvest and the wood-fired drying kilns.
body: Large cardamom is not the green cardamom of Kerala. It is a bigger, darker, smoky pod from a tall herb that grows in moist, shaded ground under trees such as alder. Sikkim has long been one of the world's main growers, and Mangan district calls itself the large cardamom capital. Many Lepcha and Nepali families around Mangan and Dzongu depend on it.

The pods grow at the base of the plant, close to the ground. Harvest starts in late August and runs through autumn. Farmers cut the clusters, separate the pods and dry them over wood fires in small kilns called bhattis. The smoke gives the spice its flavour. A good farmer can tell you the grade of a pod by look and smell.

There are no ticketed tours. Ask your hotel, a shop in the bazaar or a Dzongu homestay to introduce you to a farmer, and offer a tip of ₹200–300 for their time. Wear shoes with grip; the slopes are steep and muddy. Leeches are common in the wet season, so tuck trousers into socks.

faqs.q: What is large cardamom?
faqs.a: Large cardamom, also called black cardamom, is the large, dark, smoky pod of Amomum subulatum. It grows under shade trees in the eastern Himalaya, and Sikkim is one of its main growing areas. It is used in garam masala, biryani and meat dishes, unlike the smaller green cardamom used in sweets and tea.

faqs.q: When is cardamom harvested in Mangan?
faqs.a: Mostly from late August through October and into November, depending on altitude. Lower farms harvest earlier. September to November is the best time to see picking and the wood-fired drying kilns. Outside the season you can still see the plants and the bhattis.

faqs.q: Can I buy cardamom directly from farmers?
faqs.a: Sometimes, especially in the harvest season, though most farmers sell to traders. Shops in Mangan bazaar sell good-quality pods. Prices follow the market and swing a lot year to year; ask two or three shops before buying.

experiences.title: Momos and sel roti in Mangan bazaar
experiences.summary: Mangan's short bazaar wakes early for office staff, students and drivers. Eat steamed momos, sel roti with potato curry or a bowl of thukpa in a small eatery, then walk the shops for cardamom, ginger and whatever is in season.
body: Mangan's bazaar is not a tourist market. It serves the district: officers on their way to work, teachers, students, drivers waiting for their jeeps and families from Dzongu and the villages around. That is why breakfast here is cheap and good. Small eateries open by 7 am with tea, momos, sel roti and thukpa.

Try sel roti, the ring-shaped fried rice bread of Nepali kitchens, with aloo dum, about ₹50–80 a plate. Momos, steamed or fried, are ₹80–150 a plate; thukpa ₹100–150. Tea is ₹15–30. If you see churpi soup or local greens on the board, order them.

After breakfast walk the length of the bazaar. Shops sell large cardamom, ginger, turmeric, local oranges in winter and bamboo baskets. Ask before photographing people. It is also the best time to catch a shared jeep back to Gangtok or to bargain for a taxi across to Dzongu.

faqs.q: What is sel roti?
faqs.a: Sel roti is a ring-shaped, slightly sweet bread made from rice batter and deep-fried, common in Nepali-speaking homes across Sikkim and Darjeeling. It is eaten at breakfast with potato curry or tea and made in large quantities for festivals such as Tihar. A plate costs about ₹50–80 in Mangan.

faqs.q: Are there good places to eat in Mangan?
faqs.a: Mangan has simple eateries and hotel restaurants rather than cafes. Expect momos, thukpa, chowmein, rice-and-dal meals and sel roti, at low prices. Food is fresh because the turnover is high. Most places close early in the evening.

faqs.q: What can I buy in Mangan bazaar?
faqs.a: Large cardamom, ginger and turmeric from local farms, oranges in season, bamboo goods and everyday supplies. It is also the last good place to stock up on cash, snacks and medicines before Dzongu or the high valleys.

experiences.title: Walk up to Singhik for Kanchenjunga at dawn
experiences.summary: Singhik's viewpoint is only 4 km above Mangan. Walk up the road before sunrise on a clear morning, watch Kanchenjunga and Siniolchu catch the first light, have tea, and walk or take a taxi back to Mangan for breakfast.
body: From Mangan the road climbs gently north-west to Singhik, about 4 km away and roughly 600 m higher. Singhik is known for its view across the Teesta valley to Kanchenjunga and Siniolchu, and the walk up at dawn is the cheapest Kanchenjunga sunrise in North Sikkim.

Leave Mangan about an hour before sunrise with a torch. Walk on the road facing traffic; jeeps are few at that hour but drive fast. At Singhik the viewpoint area looks west. On clear mornings from October to April the peaks turn pink, then gold, then white. Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m, is the broad massif; Siniolchu, 6,888 m, is the sharp spire.

After sunrise, find tea in Singhik and either walk down or take a taxi, about ₹200–400. If cloud covers the peaks, try again the next morning; two dawns double your chances. Carry a warm layer, as it is cold before sunrise even at this low height.

faqs.q: How far is Singhik from Mangan?
faqs.a: About 4 km by road, roughly 1–1.5 hours on foot uphill or 10–15 minutes by taxi. Singhik is slightly higher, at around 1,560 m compared with Mangan's 956 m. The walk follows the main road, so carry a torch before dawn and watch for traffic.

faqs.q: When can I see Kanchenjunga from Singhik?
faqs.a: Clear views are most likely from October to April, especially in the early morning. Cloud often covers the peaks by mid-morning. In the monsoon, from June to September, views are rare. Plan two mornings if the view matters to you.

faqs.q: Is the road from Mangan to Singhik safe for walking?
faqs.a: Generally yes, in daylight and at dawn when traffic is light. Walk facing oncoming vehicles, wear something bright, and carry a torch before sunrise. After heavy rain, watch for loose rocks and landslide debris on the road.

experiences.title: An organic farm village above the Teesta
experiences.cost: ₹300–600 for a local guide and tea (indicative)
experiences.summary: Sikkim declared itself a fully organic farming state in 2016. Spend a morning in a village around Mangan with a local guide or homestay host to see mixed farms of cardamom, ginger, maize, vegetables and oranges, and how families live off a steep slope.
body: In 2016 Sikkim became India's first state to declare its farming fully organic, after more than a decade of phasing out chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Around Mangan this means small, mixed farms on steep terraces: cardamom under trees, ginger and turmeric, maize, millet, vegetables, mandarin oranges and a few cows or goats.

Ask your hotel in Mangan or a homestay host in Dzongu to arrange a morning with a farming family. Walk the terraces, see how water is channelled from streams, how compost is made, and what is planted when. In winter, oranges and greens; in late summer and autumn, cardamom and ginger.

There is no formal programme, so agree a modest fee in advance, ₹300–600 for a guide and tea is fair, and pay the family if they feed you. Respect fields and fences; walk on bunds, not crops. The paths are steep; wear shoes with grip and carry water.

faqs.q: Is Sikkim really fully organic?
faqs.a: Sikkim was declared a fully organic farming state in 2016, after a phased ban on chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Certification covers the state's agricultural land. In practice, around Mangan you see small mixed farms using compost and traditional methods, though enforcement and markets have their challenges.

faqs.q: Can I visit a farm near Mangan?
faqs.a: Yes, informally. Ask your hotel, a shop owner or a Dzongu homestay host to introduce you to a farming family. There are no ticketed farm tours; agree a small fee for a guide and pay for any food. September to November is the busiest time to see harvests.

faqs.q: What crops grow around Mangan?
faqs.a: Large cardamom is the main cash crop, along with ginger, turmeric, maize, millet, vegetables and mandarin oranges in lower villages. Families also keep cows, goats and poultry. Crops vary with altitude, from warm Teesta-side slopes to cooler ridges above.

faqs.q: How do I get from Gangtok to Mangan?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Gangtok's Vajra taxi stand at Maarchak, about 3 km north of the centre. Jeeps leave when full from early morning, cost about ₹200–300 a seat and take 2.5–3 hours via Kabi and Phodong. A reserved car costs about ₹2,500–3,500 one way.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Mangan?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Mangan town. Foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit for North Sikkim. Going beyond Mangan to Lachen, Lachung and the high valleys needs the North Sikkim permit, and Dzongu needs its own permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Mangan worth staying in?
faqs.a: For budget and independent travellers, yes: cheap rooms, local food, the cardamom farms, Singhik's Kanchenjunga view 4 km away and easy access to Dzongu. It is a working town, not a resort, so do not expect cafes or sightseeing infrastructure.

faqs.q: Why is North Sikkim now called Mangan district?
faqs.a: In 2021 Sikkim renamed its districts after their headquarters towns. North Sikkim district became Mangan district, East Sikkim became Gangtok district, and so on. Many people, signboards and tour operators still use the old name, North Sikkim.

faqs.q: Where do I get a Dzongu permit?
faqs.a: Dzongu permits are usually issued by the district administration in Mangan, on the same day if you arrive early with photo ID and photographs. Some homestays and Gangtok agents help arrange them in advance. Rules and offices change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs in Mangan?
faqs.a: Yes. Mangan has branches of several banks, including State Bank of India, Central Bank of India, Canara Bank and others, with ATMs in town. They are the most reliable ATMs north of Gangtok, so withdraw what you need for Dzongu or the high valleys here.

faqs.q: What is the weather in Mangan?
faqs.a: Mild compared with the high valleys. At about 956 m, winters are cool, around 6–18 °C, and summers warm and humid, up to the high 20s °C. The monsoon from June to September brings heavy rain and landslides on the Gangtok road. October to April is the most comfortable time.

faqs.q: Was Mangan affected by the 2023 Teesta flood?
faqs.a: Mangan town sits above the river and was not destroyed, but roads and bridges in the Teesta valley around it were damaged, cutting links north and south for long periods. Since then, closures after heavy rain have been frequent. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a day in Mangan cost?
faqs.a: A budget traveller can manage on about ₹1,800–2,800 a day: ₹200–300 for a shared jeep, ₹1,200–2,500 for a room, and ₹300–500 for food. Add ₹200–400 for a taxi to Singhik and a small tip if a farmer shows you around.
